articles.text: Editor: With a heavy heart I express my deep concern about the threat of a teachers’ strike in Piedmont. I genuinely appreciate the dedication of our teachers, most of whom approach their roles with passion and dedication, and I recognize the validity of their requests for increased compensation. However, I am extremely uneasy about the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) aligning with a regional coalition of unions led by the California Teachers Association (CTA). This coalition, seemingly formed just to coordinate labor action, introduces a divisive “us vs. them” mentality that betrays APT’s stated commitment to negotiate in good faith. It’s becoming increasingly clear that the list of demands that members of the Coalition have presented to their employers does not account for the unique differences of each district, budget, enrollment, or demographics. Letting outsiders drive APTs agenda is damaging to the sense of community, collaboration, and trust that makes PUSD the special district many of us moved here for. Why else would APT essentially declare in “impasse” back in August before negotiations even began? Why else would they pre-emptively authorize strike action before mediation is complete? Or before fact-finding has started? It appears that APT has no interest in negotiating, and perhaps at the direction of CTA is marching towards a strike armin-arm with other Coalition members, regardless of any offer from PUSD. Yes, our teachers deserve more. Yet, I feel strongly that the district is offering what it can to increase compensation while minimizing the impact on students. Simple math and the reality of the budget limit the district’s ability to meet all of APTs demands without cutting things that make Piedmont unique and attractive to both students and teachers who work here. For years parents have very generously supported our schools through donations and parcel taxes, but APT should not interpret this as a blank check or as unquestioning support for a strike, no matter their hardball tactics and messaging. There is a breaking point. When more families switch to private schools, more will stop donating, and the damage to the relationship between parents and teachers will become irreparable. Is APT prepared for that? –A concerned parent of two secondary students For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: And we certainly don’t want to see cuts beyond what’s being proposed, but what are we supposed to do? We’re told, don’t you understand? The district just doesn’t have enough money to help teachers with this. Well, we do understand. We see the budget numbers, and believe me, we understand the nature of the problem all too well. All of us here are intimately familiar with what it’s like not to have enough money to cover expenses. We live it every single month of our personal lives. This budget shortfall is real, but it cannot keep falling on educators’ shoulders. Many times in the past, we’ve agreed to make sacrifices to keep the district solvent. We gave up full health insurance coverage in 2011. We agreed to four straight years of furlough days after the last financial crisis. We’ve signed contract after contract below COLA [Cost of Living Adjustment] and below CPI [Consumer Price Index]. Perhaps that’s led to a tacit assumption that teachers will always somehow figure it out. Teachers are known for being able to do that. [There is] an assumption that teachers can take the hit, teachers can absorb the damage. Teachers are used to sacrificing their own well-being again and again and again. But we’ve hit a hard limit at long last. And that brings me to the announcement I have to make tonight. As many in the community are already aware, Piedmont’s educators have taken the almost unprecedented step of holding a strike authorization vote. Before I formally announce the outcome of the vote, I want to clarify what a strike authorization vote means. It is not a vote to immediately strike. Here’s the language: APT members were asked to vote yes or no on. ‘I authorize the APT Executive Board to call for a legal strike at the appropriate time if no agreement is reached once the contract bargaining process has been exhausted.’ Okay, in other words, a majority yes vote means we are still committed, as we have been, to going through the mediation process, and if necessary, the fact-finding process, with full good faith in pursuit of a fair contract resolution. However, should that process fail, a majority yes vote empowers APT leadership to call a strike at any point up until we sign a new contract. It does not have to be immediate. Again, a majority vote would be sufficient for authorization. We asked for authorization from every member of APT, and the result was overwhelming. Nearly 96% yes votes for authorization. That is an extraordinary number for Piedmont teachers. I’ve been here for 24 years. This is not a striking district, not a striking group of people, so the fact that we got 96% yes votes really tells you how desperate people are. Let me be very clear to you and to the whole community. APT’s goal will always be to avoid a strike. We want to be in the schools and classrooms teaching and supporting our students. We fully understand how disruptive a strike would be to our students. Lord knows we don’t want to lose a single minute of precious instructional time, and we don’t want our students to be stuck at home, right? We’ve all been through that, and we don’t want it again. We are deeply aware about how disruptive a strike would be to families and working parents, but we cannot sign a contract that amounts to a literal ongoing pay cut for Piedmont’s educators.”

Here’s the language: APT members were asked to vote yes or no on. ‘I authorize the APT Executive Board to call for a legal strike at the appropriate time if no agreement is reached once the contract bargaining process has been exhausted.’ Okay, in other words, a majority yes vote means we are still committed, as we have been, to going through the mediation process, and if necessary, the fact-finding process, with full good faith in pursuit of a fair contract resolution. However, should that process fail, a majority yes vote empowers APT leadership to call a strike at any point up until we sign a new contract. It does not have to be immediate. Again, a majority vote would be sufficient for authorization. We asked for authorization from every member of APT, and the result was overwhelming. Nearly 96% yes votes for authorization. This is not a striking district, not a striking group of people, so the fact that we got 96% yes votes really tells you how desperate people are. articles.text: Photo by Echa Schneider Carl Schmits, Managing Director of Equipment Standards for USA Pickleball, shows a new noise-reduced paddle. The City of Piedmont held a public demonstration of new sports equipment last week designed to reduce the sound of pickleball play. On Wednesday, January 24, at Linda Beach Courts, the city displayed newly developed sound absorption panels for noise-dampening, sound monitoring tools, and new pickleball paddles that “have been tested to reduce noise by more than 50%” according to the city. Approximately 15 people, including City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, were present at the demonstration on Wednesday, January 24. Among the more interesting equipment shown off was a remote sound monitoring service by the company SLN/CR (pronounced “silencer”). At the event, USA Pickleball representative Carl Schmits teased a SLN/ CR device that would provide real-time noise updates on local pickleball courts and, if a pre-set noise threshold was exceeded, alert city officials, club directors, and even local police departments. The device would be “plug and play,” and require very little in terms of installation or upkeep. “We’re excited to partner with USA Pickleball to showcase emerging technology and equipment at Linda Beach Courts,” said Bayon Moore. “We are a community of learners and this demonstration will accelerate our education as we continue to explore creative ways to support Piedmont’s active, engaged pickleball community while also being good neighbors.” Bayon Moore’s comment about being “good neighbors,” as well as the location of the demonstration, is likely a reference to the noise complaints of neighbors near the Linda Beach Courts. Since October 2023, the City of Piedmont has been involved with a lawsuit from a group of private citizens who claim that the City violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) by dedicating the courts without properly reviewing the noise effects it would have on the local community. Richard Drury, an attorney for the group of private citizens, said that the demonstration was a positive development for the neighborhood, but would not affect their lawsuit. “If anything, it proves that our lawsuit is meritorious,” said Drury. “We are arguing that the city should have done CEQA review to analyze feasible mitigation measures. Now the city has basically proven that we are right and there are feasible ways to reduce noise. [...] The city’s actions actually prove that they skirted the law.” As a matter of policy, the City of Piedmont does not comment on pending litigation.

articles.text: Readmont 2024, Piedmont’s community read project now in its 14th year, has selected the 2023 novel, Accountable by Dashka Slater. Slater is the New York Times–bestselling author of The 57 Bus. The author delivers a thought-provoking new young adult narrative nonfiction book about the revelation of a racist social media account that changes everything for a group of high school students and begs the question: What does it mean to be held accountable for harm that takes place behind a screen? This year’s book choice follows an event last fall when Slater was the featured speaker in an event hosted by the Piedmont Amti-Discrimination and Diversity Committee. The book is recommended for middle school students through adults. Readmont will host a community discussion featuring a panel of speakers on social media on March 6 at 7 p.m. in the Ambassador Stevens Library, 800 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont High School. English department chair Beth Black will also lead additional discussions at school during Accountable by Dashka Slater is the Readmont 2024 selection. Academy periods on March 6 and 8. articles.text: Ten Piedmont Middle School baseball players and their families will be traveling to Cuba during Spring Break, April 5-11, for a cultural exchange to see and experience the country through a love of baseball. The Piedmont team will be playing games against some of Cuba’s finest young players and will receive baseball training from experienced Cuban coaches. This trip is designed to be a once-in-a-lifetime experience for the students who will have the opportunity to play competitive baseball on Havana’s storied fields, meet and interact with Cuban youth, and develop memorable relationships. They will not only visit this beautiful island and learn about its history as they practice their Spanish speaking skills, but more importantly they will gain a valuable perspective about one of the world’s most unique countries. This exchange program is coordinated by Baseball Beyond Borders, a non-profit founded by former professional Cuban baseball player Michel Rodriguez, owner of 365 Baseball and Softball Academy. Michel started this organization to support the Cuban people and offer American kids the unique opportunity to connect with Cuban youth through a shared passion for baseball. The group is fundraising to support financial needs of players making the trip, uniforms, balls and the cost of a professional coach. Players will also be collecting baseball gear to donate to the Cuban youth baseball community. To help send the Piedmont team to Cuba and for more information, contact Mike Gray at mjgray@gmail.com. Piedmont Middle School students who will travel to Cuba during Spring Break include: Ryan McMurtry (left), Aidan Stewart, Mason Gray, Dylan Toyama, Jack Dahling, Ben McMurtry, Orion Sachs, Jonah ChaFoster, and Zachary Cha-Foster. I am a Positive Psychology and Relationship coach for neurodivergent people and anyone else who needs some help improving their lives. For those that aren’t familiar, positive psychology is a concentration within the greater field of psychology that looks at the science behind wellness and improving people’s lives. Relationships are fundamental for overall well being so much so that the World Health Organization has actually declared that loneliness is actually worse for your health than smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Since relationships are so fundamental to overall well being, I typically work on improving the relationships in my client’s lives and helping them to build new connections as well. For clients already in romantic relationships, one of the things that I work on is practicing expressing gratitude to your partner. For clients that are single and hoping to date, one of the solutions I offer is developing an understanding of one’s personal strengths throughout the dating process. Whether or not you’re in a romantic relationship, expressing gratitude to the people in your life is important. When you’ve been in a relationship for a long time, it’s easy to slip into a pattern where you’re not giving your full attention and appreciation to your partner often enough. Expressing gratitude is pretty much as simple as it sounds but remembering to do it can be more difficult. If you want to try this out, make a pact to say thank you to your partner once every day for something they’ve done or something you like about them. Strength Spotting is the practice of noticing what you are good at and then relying on that strength during difficult moments and dating is full of difficult moments. articles.text: Amelia Addington plays the role of Sally Bowles. Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret the weekend of February 1-4 at the Alan Harvey Theater. Directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead. This Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draws to a close, explores the exhilarating life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms have been omitted. Memorable songs from Cabaret include “Willkommen,” “Perfectly Marvelous,” “Money,” “Maybe This Time,” and the title song, “Cabaret”. More than 70 Piedmont and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Schultz,” said sophomore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Senior Ellie Broscow, who plays the role of Fräulein Schneider, added, “Cabaret is an incredibly important musical to me and has been for quite some time. My love for the show has definitely grown throughout the rehearsal process as I’ve realized just how relevant the themes still are, 58 years since its premiere on Broadway in 1996. The themes of anti-Semitism especially resonate with me after the events of October 7th. I have seen how the world has turned against the Jewish people throughout history, and Cabaret addresses a particularly intense period, 1929, or the rise of Hitler. The vivid anti-Semitism that existed then has continued to increase, especially right now, and we simply cannot turn a blind eye to it any longer. I hope that Cabaret will continue to be performed for years to come.” The show opens Thursday, February 1, with performances Friday through Sunday, February 2-4, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket. Performances will be held at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts, 1428 Alice Street, Oakland, on February 9-11 and 16-18. A shot at college, internet fame, and attention from the one they like – the stakes are high at Plain Springs High’s first ever Dance-a-thon. As the demonic DJ transports them to dance crazes throughout history, each contestant must face their deepest desires and greatest weaknesses. Only one couple will walk out with “The Prize” and the rest won’t make it out alive. Commissioned by YMTC in 2014, Don’t Stop Me is a musical dance-a-thon to the death from Tony Award-nominated composer/lyricist Dave Malloy and award-winning playwright and former Julliard School fellow Krista Knight. The show features 21 student actors and five creative apprentices from cities throughout the Bay Area. One adult professional Charlotte Ragones Dahlia Saffouri actor, local favorite Kevin Singer, plays the role of the disc jockey. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, including Director Jennifer Boesing, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The show includes a 7-piece pop/techno band playing Dave Malloy’s orchestrations. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $17–$38, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. YMTC offers one “pay what you will” performance on Friday, February 16, to provide affordable musical theater to all in the community. ABOUT YMTC YMTC is the Bay Area’s premiere pre-professional musical theater training organization. It brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers – as well as students of technical theater and student musicians – with professional directors, designers, choreographers and musicians.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: First-ever league win over Berkeley Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team is surging at the right time. As its season winds down, the Highlanders put themselves in position to compete for the Western Alameda County Conference title after defeating Berkeley 1-0 on Tuesday, January 23 on the road, and against Castro Valley 1-0 two days later at Chabot College in Hayward. The victory over Berkeley marks the school’s first-ever win against the Yellowjackets since joining the Western Alameda County Conference in 2012. Berkeley routinely competes for the WACC Foothill Division crown and the top division of North Coast Section. PHS, meanwhile, was recently promoted to Div. 3 in the NCS. The team’s success is a reflection of the program’s growth under eight-year head coach Todd Sullivan. “It’s a very good week,” he said. “Our win over Berkeley was the first time we’ve ever done it as a varsity program in my years. It was a huge, huge defensive effort against Berkeley and we deserved the result. We improved in the second half but just didn’t have a lot of quality. But a win is a win,” he added. Piedmont’s game-winner against Berkeley came early from Enzo Bernales in the 24th minute when cleaning up a loose ball in the box. Against Castro Valley, Aidan Woolwine scored in the first minute of second-half stoppage time at 81’. It was a miracle-goal, where Woolwine sent a cross from the right wing to the far post, the ball bounced off the turf and was mishandled by CV’s keeper who landed on the ball and punched it into net for an own goal. “It was a cross. I was looking for either Bosco [Lorin] or Enzo in the back, and I guess I hit it weird and it had some spin to it. The goalie didn’t really know what to do with it, but a goal’s a goal. We count those around here,” said Woolwine with a laugh. I am ready to get our NCS Championship run on,” said Woolwine “Berkeley is going to be looking for revenge and we learned about Bishop O’Dowd. articles.text: PHS romps: 55-20 over San Leandro, 64-47 over Castro Valley Staff Photos Natalia Martinez scored her 2,000th career point at Piedmont High School with a left-handed layup against San Leandro. Piedmont senior Natalia Martinez, a four-year starter on the basketball team, continued to etch herself into Piedmont High history. Finishing with 24 points in a 55-20 win at San Leandro on Wednesday, January 24, and officially scored her 2,000th career point for the Highlanders. She added 31 more points in a 64-47 win over Castro Valley two days later at Binks Rawlings Gym. Her record-setting 2,000th point came with 6:15 left in the fourth quarter against San Leandro after forcing a steal at midcourt, then racing to the hoop for a left-handed layup finish. “It’s going to take me a few days to process it all,” she said. “Honestly, I was going up with my left hand and I was thinking, ‘Don’t miss this.’ If this was how I’m going to do it, I thought a lefthand layup was the perfect way to get it,” she said. Martinez came to Piedmont by way of Millennium High as a freshman in 2020 and scored the historic number in her hometown of San Leandro. “It’s a reflection of how much work she’s put in and a testament to the time she’s put in,” said a proud coach, Bryan Gardere. “It’s always fun to watch players reach these different milestones and being able to celebrate it with her family and her team. It’s been a long journey. She started during COVID and had a shortened season, so she lost 10-15 games. “It’s going to be exciting to watch what she does with her career, and I’m excited for her,” Gardere added. Martinez is the second player in as many years to reach the figure after Trinity Zamora finished her career with over 2,000 points and 1,400 rebounds in 2023. Zamora is now at San Diego State, where Martinez will be playing next season. With five games left in the regular season, Piedmont holds a 15-4 overall record and is 4-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents. The team is on track for its second consecutive WACC title and a high seeding in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. Next week will be an important time to recapture the league crown. Piedmont faces Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland today, January 31, and face Alameda on Friday, February 2. 55-20 win over San Leandro Piedmont led 17-5 by the end of the first quarter and 28-8 by halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 45-13 in the third quarter, adding 10 more in the fourth while allowing seven for the 55-20 final. Martinez started the second half with eight points, but found her rhythm in the third quarter. articles.text: PHS girls post 2-0 wins over Berkeley, Castro Valley Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored both goals in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Berkeley. In a highly successful week for the Piedmont High girls’ soccer team, the Highlanders defeated Berkeley 2-0 on Tuesday, January 24 and Castro Valley 2-0 two days later. Both matches were at Chabot College in Hayward. The pair of wins brings Piedmont’s record to 8-1-3 (W-T-L) overall and 2-1-3 against league competition. Castro Valley is currently in first-place of the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division at 4-1-1, and perennial contender Berkeley is 3-0-3. PHS has three matches left in its regular season. “We’re hitting form at the right time. It’s coming together nicely,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “Our second-half against Berkeley was some of the best football I have seen us play, including from previous seasons.” Piedmont is marching towards the end of its regular season with the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs on the horizon. An added motivation will be being able to play on Witter Field after playing the full season without a home field. PHS will host its first home game at Witter on Tuesday, February 6 against Bishop O’Dowd and will honor its eight seniors on the roster. “We’ll be having our first real home game at Witter on February 6 against O’Dowd for our Senior Night. The girls are really excited to get back to Witter, we really want to get a crowd,” said Chubbock. Liu leads PHS to 2-0 over Berkeley Berkeley controlled much of the first 20 minutes, but Piedmont stabilized and began to find rhythm towards the latter portion of the first half. Piedmont came out firing in the second half and got on the board In the 50th minute when Miranda Liu scored after receiving a pass from Elsa Wallway through the back line. Liu got around Berkeley’s center back for a first-touch shot that clanged off of the left post and into net. Liu struck again in the 61st minute, this time when outside back Elle Ruegg sent a long ball from the right side over the defense. Using her speed, Liu sprinted past the defense to create a one-on-one with the goalie. She took a touch around the keeper at the top of the penalty area for an easy tap in. 2-0 over Castro Valley Both teams traded possession for the entirety of the game, and the outcome looked like it would end in a 0-0 deadlock. But with four minutes left. coach Chubbock rotated Wallway from her forward role and into Hailey Marshburn’s usual central midfield spot. Moments later, Wallway wove her way into space around the top of the penalty area, rifling a shot from distance. It forced a diving save by CV’s keeper, but the ball rebounded back it into play. Marshburn instinctively pounced on the loose ball in front of the net, slotting it into net from close range. In the final minute, Castro Valley had a last gasp at goal on Lola Beihn launched in a goal from 45 yards out against Castro Valley to give PHS a 2-0 lead. On the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park which you can reach at the end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. Hikers will be greeted to the sound of babbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls –which seemed to be the most thriving of the park after the rain. Basin Falls is about 15 feet, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet. Passing the Black Rock Falls is around 20 feet and feeds into Swanson Creek. articles.text: SF Ballet’s principal dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance in Marguerite and Armand on Wednesday, February 14. San Francisco Ballet Principal Dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance on Wednesday, February 14 at 7:30 p.m. dancing the role of Marguerite in Sir Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco from February 9 to 14. Born in Shanghai, Tan joined SF Ballet as a soloist in 1995 and was promoted to principal dancer two years later, making her the youngest and first Chinese principal dancer in the company’s history. Her unprecedented 29-year career at SF Ballet exemplified her devotion to dance and a passion to create art that is as elegant as it is human. Her repertoire has encompassed nearly 100 classical, neoclassical, and contemporary ballets choreographed by George Balanchine, Sir Kenneth MacMillan, John Neumeier, Christopher Wheeldon, Helgi Tomasson, Yuri Possokhov, Edwaard Liang, and Wayne McGregor, among others. Most notably, she has memorably interpreted classical characters such as Giselle, Aurora and Odette/Odile, as well as contemporary characters such as the Little Mermaid. As an international ambassador of ballet, she has been a symbol of ballet across the world. Since 2002, she has served as the artistic director and co-choreographer for the Tan Yuan Yuan and Her Friends production in China. In 2016, she established the Tan Yuan Yuan International Ballet Art Studio in partnership with the Shanghai Theater Academy. This community of patrons promoted ballet as a popular art form in China, enhanced cultural exchange between the U.S. and China, and gave rise to SF Ballet’s first two China tours in 2009 and 2015. Tan has been awarded the Mayor of San Francisco Art Award in 2018 and in 2022. She also received SF Ballet’s inaugural Silver Artists Society award in 2022, recognizing her 27th anniversary with the Company and longstanding contributions to SF Ballet. “Her grace, skill, versatility, and strength have helped her become the first Chinese prima ballerina in the United States and one of the greatest Chinese ballerinas of all time. She has gracefully served as a cultural ambassador for San Francisco and the U.S., said Mark Farrell, former San Francisco mayor. “I am indebted to my mentors and teachers, whose wisdom, encouragement, and belief in my potential have been instrumental in my success,” said Tan. “To my dancer colleagues, thank you for the shared moments of triumph. Through collective dedication and hard work, we have created a legacy that goes beyond individual accomplishments.” Tickets ($29-$465) to Yuan Yuan Tan’s farewell performance on February 14, or to prior performances of Marguerite and Armand February 9 to 14, may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling 415-865-2000.

articles.text: Opera San José’s 40th anniversary season continues with a thrilling production of Giuseppi Verdi’s Rigoletto, from February 17 through March 3. With some of the most memorable opera music of all time, including the signature aria “La donna è mobile,” this gripping work tells the tale of the jester Rigoletto, his innocent daughter Gilda, and the corrupt Duke of Mantua, whose callous treatment of women launches a storm of vengeance, murder and tragic self-sacrifice. The production is led by visionary director Dan Wallace Miller, acclaimed for his work with Seattle Opera and other national companies, with guest conductor Jorge Parodi making his OSJ debut. Rigoletto, Verdi’s 16th opera, is widely considered the first of the composer’s middle career masterpieces. The three-act opera made its world premiere at Teatro La Fenice in Venice, Italy on March 11, 1851, and was based on Victor Hugo’s controversial 1832 play Le Roi s’amuse (The King Amuses Himself). Set in 16th century Mantua, Italy, the opera follows a jester who struggles to balance the conflicting nature of beauty and evil in his life. “Rigoletto is one of opera’s timeless tragedies and Verdi’s most popular works as it embraces the many emotions we have as humans from cruel mockery and white-hot rage to heart-melting despair and undeniable love for family. This beloved opera is an indestructible, eternal testament to the sacrifices we make for our job, our loved ones and our honor,” said Opera San José General Director Shawna Lucey. The OSJ production features an exciting roster of talented singers, including baritone Eugene Brancoveanu in the title role of Rigoletto. Soprano Melissa Sondhi, Opera San José’s Wadhwani Artist-in-Residence who starred earlier this season as Juliet in Romeo and Juliet, returns in the role of Gilda, and tenor Edward Graves, recently seen as Gastone in San Francisco Opera’s La traviata, makes his Opera San Jose debut as the Duke of Mantua. “Classically Curious” night for Rigoletto will be held Friday, February 23, bringing together people ages 21 to 40 who are interested in deepening their involvement with opera. This program was created to introduce new audiences to opera, offering discounted tickets, behind-thescenes opportunities and social events that will connect young adult opera lovers. More information can be found at go.operasj.org/ClassicallyCurious. Tickets ($55–$195) for the performance at California Theatre (345 South 1st St., San Jose), are available at operasj.org, or by calling the box office at 408-437- 4450.

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes back Grammy-winning jazz pianist and composer Brad Mehldau to Zellerbach Hall this season for a concert on Sunday, February 10 at 8 p.m. He will perform the Bay Area premiere of his solo piano composition, 14 Reveries, along with selections from his Suite April 2020. Mehldau explores the terrain between improvisation and composition and influenced by French Impressionism. In his second performance of the 2023–24 season, he offers a recital of the work that reflects both jazz and classical influences, melding the two with pop sensibilities. “14 Reveries reflects on the interior experience we create from our own consciousness, independently of those around us... a meditation on the space a composer leaves between specific directions in the score that lets the beauty of the music reveal itself as it allows for new discovery,” he said. In a review of Mehldau’s world premiere performance of 14 Reveries in September 2023, the London Jazz News described it as “a new work which is neither straightforward nor simple, but is manifestly a very personal and special statement from one of the great musicians of our time.” As a pianist, Mehldau is widely praised for lyricism balanced with heady abstraction and innovation rooted in tradition. His influences and prolific recorded output have ventured into rock, pop, electronic music, bebop, blues and spiritual music. To date, he has released 12 trio recordings of original compositions and new arrangements of jazz standards and pop songs. He first performed at Cal Performances in 2006with the Brad Mehldau Trio with Larry Grenadier and Jeff Ballard. The group is now regarded among the great piano trios of jazz history. Tickets ($42-$98) for the show at Zellerbach Hall are available at calperformances.org, by phone at 642-9988 or in person at the ticket office Tuesday through Friday 12 to 5:30 p.m., and Saturday through Sunday 1 to 5 p.m. Cal Performances will present jazz pianist Brad Mehldau at Zellerbach Hall on Sunday, February 10.

The three-act opera made its world premiere at Teatro La Fenice in Venice, Italy on March 11, 1851, and was based on Victor Hugo’s controversial 1832 play Le Roi s’amuse (The King Amuses Himself). SF Ballet’s principal dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance in Marguerite and Armand on Wednesday, February 14. By Selen Ozturk San Francisco Ballet Principal Dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance on Wednesday, February 14 at 7:30 p.m. dancing the role of Marguerite in Sir Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco from February 9 to 14. Born in Shanghai, Tan joined SF Ballet as a soloist in 1995 and was promoted to principal dancer two years later, making her the youngest and first Chinese principal dancer in the company’s history. Her unprecedented 29-year career at SF Ballet exemplified her devotion to dance and a passion to create art that is as elegant as it is human. Her repertoire has encompassed nearly 100 classical, neoclassical, and contemporary ballets choreographed by George Balanchine, Sir Kenneth MacMillan, John Neumeier, Christopher Wheeldon, Helgi Tomasson, Yuri Possokhov, Edwaard Liang, and Wayne McGregor, among others. Most notably, she has memorably interpreted classical characters such as Giselle, Aurora and Odette/Odile, as well as contemporary characters such as the Little Mermaid. As an international ambassador of ballet, she has been a symbol of ballet across the world. Since 2002, she has served as the artistic director and co-choreographer for the Tan Yuan Yuan and Her Friends production in China. In 2016, she established the Tan Yuan Yuan International Ballet Art Studio in partnership with the Shanghai Theater Academy. This community of patrons promoted ballet as a popular art form in China, enhanced cultural exchange between the U.S. and China, and gave rise to SF Ballet’s first two China tours in 2009 and 2015. Tan has been awarded the Mayor of San Francisco Art Award in 2018 and in 2022. She also received SF Ballet’s inaugural Silver Artists Society award in 2022, recognizing her 27th anniversary with the Company and longstanding contributions to SF Ballet. “Her grace, skill, versatility, and strength have helped her become the first Chinese prima ballerina in the United States and one of the greatest Chinese ballerinas of all time. She has gracefully served as a cultural ambassador for San Francisco and the U.S., said Mark Farrell, former San Francisco mayor. “I am indebted to my mentors and teachers, whose wisdom, encouragement, and belief in my potential have been instrumental in my success,” said Tan. “To my dancer colleagues, thank you for the shared moments of triumph. Brad Mehldau at Zellerbach Hall Feb. 10 By Selen Ozturk Cal Performances welcomes back Grammy-winning jazz pianist and composer Brad Mehldau to Zellerbach Hall this season for a concert on Sunday, February 10 at 8 p.m. He will perform the Bay Area premiere of his solo piano composition, 14 Reveries, along with selections from his Suite April 2020. Mehldau explores the terrain between improvisation and composition and influenced by French Impressionism. In his second performance of the 2023–24 season, he offers a recital of the work that reflects both jazz and classical influences, melding the two with pop sensibilities. “14 Reveries reflects on the interior experience we create from our own consciousness, independently of those around us... a meditation on the space a composer leaves between specific directions in the score that lets the beauty of the music reveal itself as it allows for new discovery,” he said. In a review of Mehldau’s world premiere performance of 14 Reveries in September 2023, the London Jazz News described it as “a new work which is neither straightforward nor simple, but is manifestly a very personal and special statement from one of the great musicians of our time.” As a pianist, Mehldau is widely praised for lyricism balanced with heady abstraction and innovation rooted in tradition. articles.text: At any major U.S. museum exhibition, it is generally considered “poor form” to jump onstage, pull historic and priceless fashion pieces from their mannequins, and then try them on in a nearby mirror—usually to the horror of any nearby museum docents. Luckily, the de Young Museum has the next best thing. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style is the newest major exhibition to launch at the de Young Museum and the first ever to let audiences “try on” its dresses by using augmented reality mirrors provided on-site. The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (FAMSF) has partnered with Snap Inc., the parent company of the popular social media app Snapchat, to provide an experience they say will “bridge the gap between the digital and the physical” according to a press release. “This project showcases how Snapchat can support the arts by using augmented reality in innovative, impactful, and stylish ways,” said Rajni Jacques, Global Head of Fashion & Beauty at Snap Inc. “Our partnership with the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco is a testament to how augmented reality can infiltrate culture, encourage creativity and self-expression, and bring historic couture to life like never before.” The museum said that Fashioning San Francisco will examine the role of style as a marker of social identity. The exhibition draws mainly from the significant costume collections of the FAMSF, including a rich selection of high fashion and haute couture ensembles generously donated by Bay Area women philanthropists. The outfits featured include a 1955 “Soirée de Paris” dress by Yves Saint Laurent, a 1985 lamé outfit by San Francisco designer Kaisik Wong, and a 1987 velvet gown by Valentino. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style will be on view at the de Young Museum through August 11, 2024. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park. Tickets may be purchased online at www.famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Tickets may also be purchased in person at the admissions desk on a first-come, first-serve basis. The outfits featured in Fashioning San Francisco showcase the city’s history through its variety of trends over the years. One museum-goer “tries on” one of the dresses featured in the exhibition by using the museum’s augmented reality mirrors. ®

articles.text: The first major survey exhibition of Native Indian artist Duane Linklater is on view at Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) through February 25. Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will present the first major survey exhibition of Canadian Duane Linklater, the celebrated Omaskêko Ininiwak artist whose work explores the contradictions of contemporary Native Indian life. The exhibit Duane Linklater: mymothersside features more than 30 works by this artist, who has over the past decade become a leading voice in the contemporary art world, with important contributions to the 2022 Whitney Biennial and the 2023 Bienal de Saõ Paulo, in Brazil. The exhibition will survey the wide scope of Linklater’s practice, which encompasses painting, sculpture, video and performance. Based in North Bay, Ontario, Linklater has been celebrated for a conceptual and material practice that interrogates what he calls “the physical and theoretical structures of the museum” in relation to the exclusion of indigenous cultures past and present. His work references ancestral traditions from Moose Cree First Nation – from hunting to fur trading to berry gathering – alongside popular bands and films of his youth, including the English rock band The Cure and the American blues musician Taj Mahal. The exhibit includes structures made with teepee poles, highlighting the artist’s interest in reassembling one of the most ubiquitous symbols of Indigeneity. The large-scale architectural installations will be displayed alongside Linklater’s draped and folded teepee cover paintings, shaped canvases the artist uses a combination of digital printing and natural dyeing techniques. “We’re thrilled to partner with Duane Linklater on bringing his first survey museum exhibition to Berkeley, which will give our audiences the opportunity to discover one of today’s most vital and engaging artists,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director Julie Widholm. “Duane’s interest in reimagining the role of Indigenous art in traditional museum spaces engages the critical questions we want to explore at BAMPFA.” Berkeley Art Museum is located at 2155 Center Street on the UC Berkely campus. Hours of operation are 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($14 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa.org, or in-person at the museum desk.

This vibrant and romantic concert will feature piano trios exploring a wide range of French music, including Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Trio No. 1 in D Minor; Arthur Honegger’s Sonatine for Violin and Cello; Bay Area composer Jean Ahn’s A Flashback of Ravel; and Claude Debussy’s Piano Trio in G Major. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate the Lunar New Year with their Year of the Dragon concert and banquet with 4 p.m. pre-concert festivities, a 5 p.m. performance and a 6:30 p.m. post-concert feast on Saturday, February 17 at Davies Symphony Hall. Lunar New Year is the most important holiday for many cultures in East, South and Southeast Asia, and is celebrated by people of Asian descent worldwide. This year’s celebration marks the 24th anniversary of the SF Symphony’s signature event, an elegant celebration of the Lunar New Year drawing upon vibrant Asian traditions past and present. The celebration begins at 4 p.m. with pre-concert lobby festivities open to all ticket holders, featuring an array of entertainment and activities including dragon dancers, fortune readers, calligraphy artists, and cultural performances. Conductor Mei-Ann Chen and the orchestra will then open the concert with Li Huan-Zhi’s energetic Spring Festival Overture and Phoon Yew Tien’s joyful New Year Greetings. The orchestra will then perform Jasmine Flower, a folk song from China’s Jiangsu province, which was arranged for orchestra by Li Wenping in 1999. The program continues with Flower Drum Song from Feng Yang and Girl from Da Ban City from Huang Ruo’s Folk Songs for Orchestra, originally commissioned and performed by the San Francisco Symphony at their 2012 Chinese New Year concert. Also on the program is Vivian Fung’s Pizzicato, which features sounds inspired by two Chinese instruments — the pipa and qin — as well as Indonesian gamelan music. Violinist Paul Huang will join the Symphony to play music from Tan Dun’s violin concerto, Fire Ritual, originally written for and premiered by violinist Eldbjørg Hemsing. Concluding the program are Che Chang’s Ali Mountain Evergreen, a piece that evokes the staggering scale of Ali Mountain in Taiwan, and Chen Ge Xin’s Gong Xi Gong Xi, a popular Chinese Lunar New Year song that translates to “Congratulations” or “Wishing You Happiness and Prosperity.” The post-concert Lunar New Year Banquet begins at 6:30 p.m. in Zellerbach Rehearsal Hall, located at 300 Franklin Street at the rear of Davies Symphony Hall. This event will feature a lucky draw and live music. The banquet will be catered by McCalls Catering & Events, with lighting design by Got Light. The décor for the event will feature hanging screens that highlight the many ways that Lunar New Year is celebrated across different cultures. Proceeds from the event support the Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. Tickets for the concert ($39- $109) and information about individual and full banquet table reservations can be found for purchase at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415- 864-6000. San Francisco Symphony’s Lunar New Year concert returns on Saturday, February 17.

articles.text: And it is in this sweet spot that Stephen King resides, coming at it from a myriad of angles with a prolific talent that seems without end. What King understands, and this is his genius, is that it is part of human nature to carry a nugget of unresolved uneasiness, of a willingness to suspend one’s disbelief, and enter into that dark geography that haunted us as kids. It’s why standing on the top step of a dark basement, the ominous smells wafting up, then turning on the light switch and finding that the lights aren’t working so resonates. And therein is the power and effectiveness of the film It. Using the image of the benign and joyful clown, King takes the expected and transforms it into the most frightful. Part of the brilliance of this film, set in the small town of Derry, Maine in 1989, is that it opens with seven middle-schoolers, all just released from school with the summer stretching before them. At the outset they are not a crew, though each resides on that outcast edge of the school experience. articles.text: Thomasin McKenzie and Ben Foster in Leave No Trace Leave No Trace opens with a father, Will (Ben Foster), and his teenage daughter, Tom (Thomasin McKenzie), preparing chopped kindling for a fire. Slowly the camera pulls back and it gradually becomes obvious that where they are staying is not a temporary shelter, erected for one night before moving on. There is a permanence to what is revealed: a tent, a canopy of tarps, one to trap rainwater, a small butane cook stove; this is home. The place is Forest Park, a 5,000-acre wilderness just outside Portland, Ore., and Will and Tom are, in effect living off the grid. It’s an interesting distinction, the term “living off the grid,” and being homeless, living on the urban streets of a city like Portland. For Will and Tom, it’s a purposeful choice to live in a place apart and for them being “off the grid” is a term of art, a philosophy, a value judgment as well as a kind of lifestyle shorthand. And so, stripped of all extraneous societal distractions, Leave No Trace has at its center the tender and subtle relationship between father and daughter as they go about their self-sufficient days, gathering mushrooms, greens, preparing meals, rehearsing what they must do if discovered by “them.” On occasion, they walk into town to buy necessary supplies using money Will receives from selling his veteran PTSD meds to homeless vets. As for backstory, the cause of Will’s intentional retreat, with Tom, into the woods, is only hinted at. There is a moment, in the dead of night, when he wakes to the sound of a helicopter overhead that only he can hear. Hyperventilating, he struggles to find firm ground. It is Will who has constructed their lives as they are, to leave as soft a trace as possible. And Tom mirrors his gentle spirit, something that is reflected in their spare conversation and silent interaction all of which convey the depth and strength of their bond as well as their fundamental kindness. And it is that bond that frames this remarkable and moving film, an allegory, a poem, really, so beautifully made, so intimately told, so universal, an exemplum of how life can ever so unexpectedly shift the prism through which we observe its elusive meaning. Tension is introduced when the “the grid” intrudes into Tom and Will’s delicately eco-balanced lives. It is painful to watch as Tom opens up to other aspects of life and to community while Will’s reflexive reaction is to retreat. Leave No Trace is directed by Debra Granik whose breakout film was Winter’s Bone. She is a gifted filmmaker who can capture in image and interaction the muted vagaries of the human condition, most especially that period in a young person’s life often referred to as the rite of passage. The performances offered by Ben Foster, one of the best actors working today, and Thomasin McKenzie, a Kiwi who is new to Hollywood, are simply exceptional. Each is able to capture with a subdued expression, a discerning glance, emotions that require no exposition. Even for Will it is impossible to go through life in the presence of others and leave no trace. This is a truth that bears down on him; however, at great personal cost, he still must try. Leave No Trace. Directed by Debra Granik, Starring Ben Foster, Thomasin McKenzie, Jeff Kober. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/apple tv.

articles.text: Let’s say you’re about 12 or 13 and looking to spend a couple of hours being severely entertained, wanting the world outside to drop away, the demands of peers and school to vanish. What better way to escape than to scrunch down on the sofa and watch Race to Witch Mountain starring Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock. Witch Mountain is a smorgasbord of stuff that kids enjoy: two teenage ETs, Sara (AnnaSophia Robb) and Seth (Alexander Ludwig), whose space craft crashes on earth, and are desperate to return home. Government agents, led by Burke (Cirian Hinds), having recovered their ship and are in the hunt to find the aliens so they can study them in a federal facility. Plus there’s an alien ironclad terminator sent to kill them; a super-sized father figure in the form of Jack Bruno (Johnson) who has taken them under his muscular wing. There are lots of edgy chase scenes and close calls; an ET/SF Las Vegas convention with tons of Trekies and Star War geeks; and loads of piled-on special effects. Just perfect. Of course, kids will watch Race to Witch Mountain uncritically, ignoring the lame plot and dialogue. Nor will said filmgoers point out to their peers that Seth and Sara, who have a truckload of ET powers, don’t always use their powers, even when in a really, really tight spot. Case in point would be Sara, who can shoot energy bolts using the tip of her finger and holds off, even with the Feds closing in. Wouldn’t you use the standby energy bolt? But no matter, this is a spiffy movie that will keep young moviegoers pretty much riveted. Race to Witch Mountain. Directed by Andy Fickman. Starring Dwayne Johnson, AnnaSophia Robb, Alexander Ludwig, Carla Gugino and Cirian Hinds. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ prime/Disney+/apple tv. Plus there’s an alien ironclad terminator sent to kill them; a super-sized father figure in the form of Jack Bruno (Johnson) who has taken them under his muscular wing. There are lots of edgy chase scenes and close calls; an ET/SF Las Vegas convention with tons of Trekies and Star War geeks; and loads of piled-on special effects. Just perfect. But no matter, this is a spiffy movie that will keep young moviegoers pretty much riveted. Race to Witch Mountain. Directed by Andy Fickman. Thomasin McKenzie and Ben Foster in Leave No Trace By Chris Honoré Leave No Trace opens with a father, Will (Ben Foster), and his teenage daughter, Tom (Thomasin McKenzie), preparing chopped kindling for a fire. Slowly the camera pulls back and it gradually becomes obvious that where they are staying is not a temporary shelter, erected for one night before moving on. There is a permanence to what is revealed: a tent, a canopy of tarps, one to trap rainwater, a small butane cook stove; this is home. The place is Forest Park, a 5,000-acre wilderness just outside Portland, Ore., and Will and Tom are, in effect living off the grid. It’s an interesting distinction, the term “living off the grid,” and being homeless, living on the urban streets of a city like Portland. For Will and Tom, it’s a purposeful choice to live in a place apart and for them being “off the grid” is a term of art, a philosophy, a value judgment as well as a kind of lifestyle shorthand. And so, stripped of all extraneous societal distractions, Leave No Trace has at its center the tender and subtle relationship between father and daughter as they go about their self-sufficient days, gathering mushrooms, greens, preparing meals, rehearsing what they must do if discovered by “them.” On occasion, they walk into town to buy necessary supplies using money Will receives from selling his veteran PTSD meds to homeless vets. As for backstory, the cause of Will’s intentional retreat, with Tom, into the woods, is only hinted at. There is a moment, in the dead of night, when he wakes to the sound of a helicopter overhead that only he can hear. Hyperventilating, he struggles to find firm ground. It is Will who has constructed their lives as they are, to leave as soft a trace as possible. And Tom mirrors his gentle spirit, something that is reflected in their spare conversation and silent interaction all of which convey the depth and strength of their bond as well as their fundamental kindness. And it is that bond that frames this remarkable and moving film, an allegory, a poem, really, so beautifully made, so intimately told, so universal, an exemplum of how life can ever so unexpectedly shift the prism through which we observe its elusive meaning. Tension is introduced when the “the grid” intrudes into Tom and Will’s delicately eco-balanced lives. It is painful to watch as Tom opens up to other aspects of life and to community while Will’s reflexive reaction is to retreat. The performances offered by Ben Foster, one of the best actors working today, and Thomasin McKenzie, a Kiwi who is new to Hollywood, are simply exceptional. Each is able to capture with a subdued expression, a discerning glance, emotions that require no exposition. Even for Will it is impossible to go through life in the presence of others and leave no trace. This is a truth that bears down on him; however, at great personal cost, he still must try. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Spanish-style Red Lentil Soup is a classic warm meal on a cold winter night. This is the time of year when we look to lighten up our meals and lighten up cooking duties after months of large holiday meals. This soup checks the boxes for both and can be made from a well-stocked Piedmont pantry. Bonus: it scales up nicely to feed a crowd! The list of ingredients looks long, but many of the items are “staples” in many kitchens. The spices and even vegetables can be changed up to suit your taste. I’m not a fan of cooked carrots; I think they can take the dish in a too-sweet direction. But if that’s what you love about carrots, then you know what to do… Note: Soaking the saffron in liquid (wine or water) in preparation for cooking is called “blooming”, which draws the most flavor out of the most expensive spice (by weight) in the world. Spanish-Style Red Lentil Soup Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 1 medium onion, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 2 stalks celery, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 1 red pepper, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 2 small carrots, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1/ 2 cup • 3 – 4 cloves garlic, minced, about 1 tablespoon • 1 bay leaf • 2 teaspoons Mediterranean oregano, dried • 1 tablespoon sweet paprika • 1 teaspoon smoked paprika • 1/2 teaspoon piment d’esplette, or to taste (substitute cayenne pepper) • 1/8 teaspoon saffron threads, crumbled and “bloomed” in 2 tablespoons of dry white wine or water • 1 can diced tomatoes, 14.5 ounces (Use fire-roasted for extra flavor, but regular are fine.) • • • • • • 1-1/2 cups dried red lentils 1 quart low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth 2 cups of water, or as needed to obtain desired consistency Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste Fresh lemon wedges and additional extra-virgin olive oil to drizzle at serving Parsley for garnish INSTRUCTIONS Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a 4-quart saucepan over medium-high heat until it just begins to shimmer. Add the onion and celery, stir together and sauté until softened – about 3 minutes. Add the red pepper, carrots, and garlic and continue cooking until the all are softened and aromatic – another 3–4 minutes. Add the bay leaf, oregano, both paprikas, and piment d’esplette, then stir well to combine. Add in the saffron and the blooming liquid, and canned diced tomatoes. Finally add the 1-quart of stock and 2 cups of water. Stir all to combine well. Cover and bring to a slow boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer until the lentils are tender, about 20-30 minutes. With an immersion blender, use short bursts to coarsely puree the soup. Alternatively, remove about half of the soup to a food processor or regular blender and pulse a few times to achieve a coarse texture. Add the pureed portion back to the pot. The soup should be a bit chunky. Taste and adjust seasonings to suit. Ladle the soup into bowls, then drizzle with olive oil and a spritz of fresh lemon juice. Garnish with flat-leaf parsley and serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 8, 2020.

articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson We all know that winter isn’t peak fruit season. Yes, this time of year brings plenty of citrus, and one can certainly harvest what the French call les fruits de mer, including delightful Dungeness crab. But don’t be fooled by the paucity of locally grown fruit at the grocery store. Now is the perfect time to start planting and pruning fruit trees in your garden. A few winters ago, I ordered bare-root fruit trees through the mail. I was nervous. It seemed counterintuitive that one could ship saplings halfway across the country without soil. It took me a week to get around to planting them, and then I had to wait two months to see what would happen. I was pleasantly surprised – they all leafed out beautifully. Bare-root fruit trees usually cost less than the ones in pots and are almost as easy to plant. The hole you dig should be twice as wide as the spread of the tree’s roots but not too deep. To keep the bare roots from compacting, ask a friend to hold the tree in place while you fill in the soil. Make a mound with a donut around it to catch irrigation water. Ideally, the trunk will be one to two inches above ground level once you fill in the soil. I’ve been particularly happy with my bare-root apple trees. The variety known as Arkansas Black, as the name suggests, has a deep purple skin that is nearly black at maturity. In keeping with the French / espalier theme, Diane Louvel, a French friend visiting from New York, stands next to a cherry tree. Josh Harkinson stands next to an apple tree with espalier. The Pink Pearl, a yellow apple with strikingly pink flesh, was developed in 1944 by Northern California breeder Albert Etter by crossing a conventional apple with red-fleshed Russian crab apple. Both varieties grew quickly, fruited profusely in the second year, and taste great. Fruit trees don’t necessarily require a lot of space. During the Middle Ages, Europeans wanted to plant them inside castle courtyards. The technique they developed, now known as espalier, is a French word deriving from the Italian spalliera, meaning “something to rest the shoulder (spalla) against.” It refers to the trellises that train the branches of fruit trees to grow horizontally, but there are also espalier techniques that require little in the way of infrastructure. Espalier works best with apples and pears. I planted my apple trees next to a waist-high picket fence and allowed them to shoot straight up. After they’d shed their leaves for the winter, I bent the branches sideways until they were parallel with the fence and secured them with twine. The following winter, I pruned to maintain the two-dimensional shape. I cut off most of the twigs but retained some of the tallest new shoots – two- or three-feettall growths from the original espaliered branches – and bent them back the other direction, securing them with twine. After a couple of years, I had a living fence that was more than six feet tall. For other types of fruit, you can often find dwarf varieties adapted to our climate. It’s a bit too cold in this part of the East Bay for sweet cherries, but I have a dwarf sour cherry tree that produces bucketloads of fruit every year and makes fantastic pies. And while pomegranates also prefer more heat than we get, I planted a pomegranate hedge on the south-facing edge of my driveway, which acts like a heat island. After about five years it has started to yield some great fruit. The only problem comes in late fall when I must choose between scratching my car or lopping off some nice pomegranates before they’ve ripened. As the French and Americans would say, c’est la vie. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening.

articles.text: A few longtime members of the Piedmont Seniors celebrate the holiday season at the Claremont Country Club. On December 14, a total of 50 Piedmont Seniors and guests had a special holiday luncheon at Claremont Country Club. The Garden Room was festively decorated with strands of garlands attached to the ceiling as well as a colorful Christmas tree by the fireplace. The occasion was augmented by a pianist who played both holiday and other well-known tunes. Adding to the festivities, there was an optional gift exchange where the group selected wrapped packages with others who brought gifts to swap. The luncheon consisted of butternut squash soup, cordon blue chicken breast, spinach and mushroom crepes, and ice cream dosed with chocolate sauce. To make this get-together even sweeter there were assorted holiday candies at each place setting. This luncheon has become an annual tradition, as the Piedmont Seniors look forward to marking the holiday season each year. The Seniors have been going to the Claremont County Club during the holidays for approximately 20 years. The Claremont Country Club was established in 1897 and has become a favorite spot as it is conveniently located near Piedmont and upper Rockridge areas. The Claremont’s Tudor style clubhouse has become a sanctuary for those seeking a respite from the “hustle and bustle” of everyday life. If you are interested in learning more about the Piedmont Seniors, including meetings and excursions, contact Janet Epstein, Coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.us. The Seniors are a very welcoming group and are always looking to meet new members. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to participate in the activities. Pictured are Jim Ayotte (left), Gregory Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Mona Jamieson, and Fred Pemberton. Dear MacMama: I just brought home a new MacBook Air, and the salesperson at the Apple store told me I can use iCloud to sync my items from my older computer to my new one. How does that work exactly? I don’t actually understand how iCloud works. –Oliver D., Piedmont Dear Oliver: Simply said, Apple’s iCloud is a storage service that can both store your files and sync them across all your devices. But there is much more to iCloud. We use it to sync contacts, reminders, calendars, and photos. We use it to store documents, folders, and passwords. If your computer has OS Catalina or later, when you turn on location services, you can use it to find misplaced iPhones, air pods, and Apple watches. If we use Air Tags, we can keep track of almost any item like wallets, keys, and anything to which we can attach an Air Tag. If your older Mac had OSX Yosemite or later, you can turn on iCloud Drive, enable “Desktop and Documents” and then all items on your desktop and in your “documents” folder will be stored in iCloud. They will still exist on your computer, and any other device in which you were signed in with the same Apple ID and have enabled iCloud Drive. This is great for people who have more than one device and need to keep their files in sync. So, for example, since I have iCloud enabled, if I work on a file in one computer, as soon as my other computer connects to the Internet, that file will be updated. And all my files are on both machines. If the operating system on your old computer is current enough and iCloud is enabled, you can set up the new computer, sign into iCloud, and these files will be downloaded onto your new computer. The same goes for photos, contacts and calendars. But this is not a complete solution for moving all your data over. For example, if you purchased Microsoft applications, Adobe applications, any non-Apple applications that don’t come on your machine from the factory, these will not transfer over with iCloud. And if you organize your mail into local folders, meaning the folders that exist in Apple Mail under the heading “On My Mac”, these will also not transfer over. So, in some cases, using Time Machine (assuming you have been backing up your old machine with Time Machine to an external drive) is a better way to transfer your data from an old machine to a new one. There are so many features in iCloud that it would take much more than this column to explain them all. Even if you use Time Machine on an external drive from your previous computer, in many cases, it is still prudent to enable iCloud to store and sync your desktop and documents. This acts as a cloud back up and makes these files accessible on your iPhone and iPad on the “Files” app, assuming the operating system on your device is current enough. There have been so many times that I have been without my computer, and somebody needs a file very quickly, and I have been able to email it by accessing my computer files right from my iPhone. Of course, keeping all our personal data, as well as sensitive data in a cloud storage system has its risks. Although Apple takes privacy seriously and protects your information by encrypting it when it’s in transit and storing it in an encrypted format, there are always security risks. It’s really important to use a secure password for your Apple/iCloud ID. It’s not just Apple that has security risks. Dropbox, Google Drive, any cloud storage is vulnerable to security breaches. But used wisely, with a good secure password, iCloud can be a real timesaver.. articles.text: It had rained earlier in the morning and it looked like there could be some more last Wednesday, however, the uncertain weather didn’t stop 24 walkers and one K-9 best friend from a stroll in central Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesday group decided to revisit the history of Walter Blair, the first European settler on the area, and go the site of his original Blair’s Park on what is now the north side of Moraga Avenue. This park was an attraction Blair created to get people to come to his Piedmont Springs Hotel that he built in 1872, and where the Exedra is today. Blair came to California from Vermont during the gold rush in 1852 at the age of 22 with $100. In 1852 he purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. His land was most of the area between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original home was where 111 Highland Avenue is today with its back on today’s Waldo Avenue. He started as a dairy farmer and established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues. His cattle grazed in pastures that ran to Grand Avenue. He also developed a quarry where Dracena Park is today. The walkers went down Highland Avenue and found the site of Blair’s home. When they got to the end of the street more of Blair’s history was shared. He was an entrepreneur and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 he decided to build his own line from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery to the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase ridership in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, which he named “Blair’s Park.” It had an entrance arch at what is now the corner of Highland and Moraga Avenues and offered many ascensions. Many of these picnickers and hotel guests purchased land and became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair died in 1888 and was only 57 years old. Blair Avenue in Piedmont is named for him. After his death Blair Park was purchased in 1890 by a company that operated a cable car up Oakland Avenue. However, the company went into receivership in 1893. Blair’s heirs owned the park land, but in 1897 all of Blair’s remaining 235 acers, including Blair’s Park, were for sale. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and in 1902 Frank C. Havens’ land development syndicate owned the park land. By 1913 the land was vacant, but in 1917 builder Guy Turner built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue and at least six more in 1922. The walkers looked across Moraga Avenue where the original entrance to Blair Park was located and took a group photo. They made their way down Moraga passing Turner’s homes and came to the gate entrance of a nine-unit apartment building that was built in 1914. Two gardeners were working in the yard, and the group asked if they could come in. Permission was granted and the group enjoyed Walter Blair the beautiful garden and view of San Francisco. The group continued down Moraga to the Oakland/Piedmont city line at Pleasant Valley Avenue, and went on Ronada Avenue, to Parkside Drive cul-de-sac, and then up to Ronada, Ramona, and Estrella Avenues. A right on Bonita Avenue and a left on Park Way brought got the walkers to Waldo and Blair Avenues, and a chance to once again remember Walter Blair. They arrived back at the Exedra just as the moisture could no longer to be called mist. The group had escaped the rain and enjoyed a fun three-mile walk and an almost entirely dry morning together. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Number 11 streetcar on the right-of-way between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues in 1948. was what then was the newly built Transbay Terminal in San Francisco. Cars travelled east and west on the top level of the bridge. Electric trains served other parts of the East Bay. The A Train covered downtown Oakland, and the B Train travelled through the Lakeshore and Trestle Glen neighborhoods. The E Train went to Berkeley to the Claremont Hotel. In Berkeley, the F Train travelled on Shattuck to Solano, the G Train served Westbrae, the H Train travelled on Monterey Avenue, and the K Train ran on College Avenue. Today, some AC Transit buses use the same letters to identify their routes. End of the Line The last Piedmont streetcar operated until 1948. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. The C Train continued to run to San Francisco until 1958 when streetcars on the Bay Bridge were discontinued. The Oakland Tribune described this poignant time as “sad, exuberant, quiet, noisy, confused and orderly.” That last ride was standing room only. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. The C Train at the small Oakland Avenue station at Latham that provided shelter to waiting passengers in 1940. Legacy The Number 11 and 12 streetcar lines and the C Train also left a legacy of vacant right-ofway land. The right-of-way for the Number 11 between Sunnyside and Linda became the beautifully landscaped Linda Park and the energetic Linda Avenue Dog Park across from Beach School. The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue had no dedicated right-of-way. When the C Train stopped running, its right-of-ways were filled with houses. Today, three narrow houses occupy the right-of-way along Latham. The land between Ricardo and York became more back yard space for adjacent houses. New houses were built on York near Arroyo. The C Train also shared the right-of-way on Arroyo with the Number 10 streetcar before it As the C Train curves to the right toward its route to Latham and Oakland, the Number 10 streetcar descends Arroyo toward Piedmont Avenue.

articles.text: Part 2 of a two-part series. (Part 1 was reprinted on January 10, 2024.) My prev ious colu m n described the Number 10 streetcar line in Piedmont. It was the longest Key Route line in Piedmont and ran from Piedmont Avenue and 41st to Crocker Park. There were two other streetcar lines and an electric train in Piedmont that provided convenient, reliable and inexpensive transportation to other neighborhood cities, downtown Oakland and San Francisco. The Number 11 streetcar ran from 7th and Broadway in Oakland up Oakland Avenue into Piedmont. At the Oakland Avenue Bridge it turned left and continued onto the rightof-way that ran between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues. At Lake Avenue, the streetcar ran on Linda Avenue to Piedmont Avenue and to the end of its line at the Piedmont Avenue Station. (The route up Oakland Avenue from Grand Ave. was too steep for electric streetcars.) The Number 12 streetcar also traveled from downtown Oakland, but it served another part of Piedmont. It ran up Grand Avenue and up Fairview Avenue beside the strip park. It ended at Oakland and Jerome Avenues. From there, passengers could cross Oakland Avenue to board the C Train to San Francisco. Taking the C Train to San Francisco When the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, the Key System added electric train service to San Francisco. (The Key Route had became the Key System in 1923.) The electric C Train began service to Piedmont in 1939 and offered direct transportation from Piedmont to San Francisco every 20 minutes. Each train had a smoking section and “card tables were provided for commuters used to such diversions when they rode the ferries.” Many Piedmont commuters caught the C Train from the small Spanish-style waiting station at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street. From there the train travelled along Latham, then between the houses on Ricardo and York. Two stops allowed more passengers to board before the train left Piedmont for the station at 41st Street and Piedmont Ave. and on to the Bay Bridge. The lower level of the new Bay Bridge was reserved for trucks and trains. The electric trains ran on parallel tracks on the south side of the bridge, and trucks used the north side. Each train had a smoking section and “card tables were provided for commuters used to such diversions when they rode the ferries.” Many Piedmont commuters caught the C Train from the small Spanish-style waiting station at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street. From there the train travelled along Latham, then between the houses on Ricardo and York. Two stops allowed more passengers to board before the train left Piedmont for the station at 41st Street and Piedmont Ave. and on to the Bay Bridge. The lower level of the new Bay Bridge was reserved for trucks and trains. The electric trains ran on parallel tracks on the south side of the bridge, and trucks used the north side. The end of the line for the C Train The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue in 1943.
